title: Stereotypes, Prejudice & Discrimination
degreeAttributes: Social & Beh Sci - Beh Sci, and Cultural Studies - US Minority course.
info: Prerequisite: This course is intended for first and second year students.

sections.sectionText: Exploration of the issues and methods necessary to understand and conduct research into stereotyping, prejudice, and discrimination. To achieve this goal, the course will be broken up into three sections. In the first section, students will be introduced to the basic methods of how behavioral scientists develop research questions, conduct studies, reach conclusions about their findings, and ultimately generalize their findings to understand human behavior. In the second section, students will read about and discuss research examining stereotyping, prejudice, and discrimination, and how these factors contribute to inequality. In the final section, students will learn about research that translates basic findings from behavioral science to understand real-world consequences of stereotyping, prejudice, and inequality. Throughout the course, students will have opportunities to experience the inner workings of the behavioral science research process through touring UIUC behavioral science laboratories, completing and discussing measures of stereotyping and bias employed in the behavioral sciences, and designing and proposing their own empirical studies that would address questions related to inequality. Restricted to Chancellor's Scholars in the Campus Honors Program (CHP).

sections.sectionText: Multiculturalism in Clinical-Community Research and Practice- Multiculturalism is a popular topic and as aspiring psychologists it is important to stay up to date with its meaning and implications: personally, as a helping professional, in your research, and in your practice. In this course, we will discuss and define multiculturalism, understand individuals and your own reactions to multiculturalism, and discuss foundational frameworks that guide diverse approaches to integrating multiculturalism in clinical and community research and practice. This course involves reading required assignments, active class participation, and consistent completion of writing activities. Final grading for this course will be based on points earned for active class participation, completing assigned readings, writing assignments, literature reviews, topic development proposals, a final paper proposal, and a final individual poster presentation. sections.sectionText: Course title: Introduction to Computational Neuroscience This course aims to provide an introduction to computational neuroscience. It will review the computational tools used for analyzing neural data and the principal theories of how the brain performs computations. The course will introduce students to topics in linear algebra, differential equations, and probability & statistics, with a heavy emphasis on applications to neurobiology. The course will seek to give students both a good intuitive understanding and a practical mastery of various mathematical and computational methods, and equip them with programming and data visualization skills that are increasingly important to scientific inquiry in general, and neuroscience in particular. Students will program in Python, and homework problem sets will focus heavily on programming. Experience with programming in Python is helpful but not required; expect to put in additional time to get up to speed if no experience programming. sections.sectionText: Schoolyards and Prison Yards: Restorative Justice in Mainstream Systems Building on the foundation developed in PSYC 339: Restorative Justice: Principles and Methods, this course examines the use of restorative justice in two different systemic contexts. The first part explores restorative justice approaches in educational settings, including building and strengthening relationships as well as restorative responses to conflicts and violations of school norms and rules. In the second half, we'll examine conventional responses to crime and look at early attempts at restorative justice within and in place of the criminal justice response. Although the focus will be on exploring theoretical, empirical, and experiential writings concerning restorative approaches, there will also be some opportunity to develop and practice applied "facilitation" skills. To the extent possible within the structure of the university system, the course itself will be guided by restorative principles, including power sharing. Students enrolling in this course will have either taken the RJ Principles and Methods course or have other previous experience or familiarity with restorative justice. Schoolyards and Prison Yards: Restorative Justice in Mainstream Systems Building on the foundation developed in PSYC 339: Restorative Justice: Principles and Methods, this course examines the use of restorative justice in two different systemic contexts. The first part explores restorative justice approaches in educational settings, including building and strengthening relationships as well as restorative responses to conflicts and violations of school norms and rules. In the second half, we'll examine conventional responses to crime and look at early attempts at restorative justice within and in place of the criminal justice response. Although the focus will be on exploring theoretical, empirical, and experiential writings concerning restorative approaches, there will also be some opportunity to develop and practice applied "facilitation" skills. To the extent possible within the structure of the university system, the course itself will be guided by restorative principles, including power sharing. Students enrolling in this course will have either taken the RJ Principles and Methods course or have other previous experience or familiarity with restorative justice.

Computational Foundations for Behavioral Science This course teaches the fundamentals of computer programming with Python to achieve research goals as a behavioral scientist. We will cover implementing experiments, data analyses, simulations, and computational models in the behavioral and social sciences. By the end of the course, students will have developed a piece of software (such as an experiment or in-depth set of analyses) that substantively advances their own ongoing research programs, as well as a manuscript proposing (or elucidating the results of) said experiment/analyses. Core topics include program design, data wrangling and visualization, reproducible workflows (version control, environments), experiment/game scripting, statistical modeling, and simple machine-learning pipelines. Prior coding experience not required; familiarity with quantitative research methods recommended. Intended for graduate students in psychology/cognitive science, neuroscience, economics, sociology, political science, and related fields. Meets with BCOG 200. Graduate students should register for this section. MSPS Students need to register for this course.

sections.sectionText: This seminar examines how social and psychological processes shape physical and mental health, exploring topics such as stress and coping, chronic illness, health disparities, and pain. Students will engage with the primary research literature to discuss how social psychology can inform research and practices in health contexts. This seminar is tailored to students with interests in social psychology, clinical and health sciences, or applied disciplines focusing on physical or mental health.

This seminar focuses on issues of diversity and multiculturalism and their impact on theory, research, and practice in clinical and community psychology. Seminar topics are wide ranging and presentations vary in format from lectures to workshops.

Course Description: This seminar course examines the role of macronutrients and micronutrients in the development, prognosis, and therapeutic management of psychiatric, neurodevelopmental, and neurodegenerative conditions including but not limited to affective disorders, autism spectrum disorders, and cognitive decline. The seminar begins with introductory literature reviews to establish fundamental concepts and methodological paradigms. Following this orientation, interactive, student-driven discussions will focus on contemporary clinical and pre-clinical research articles. By the end of this course, students will be able to (1) critique scientific literature, (2) delineate underlying mechanisms, (3) apply the knowledge and design studies to address related research questions.

Topic: Diversity and Inclusion Considerations in Cognitive Psychology This course will provide students with knowledge on foundational and cutting-edge research in the field of cognitive psychology. In addition, we will examine and critique the ways that research conducted in cognitive psychology has handled issues related to diversity and inclusion. Finally, we will consider how this research area can be more diverse and inclusive in the future.

The goal of this course is for students to acquire skills and learn good practices for the use of tools for reproducible research, data management, and effective visualizations. Good practices for reproducible research involve setting up an analysis workflow that uses literate statistical analysis tools and implements conscientious data management strategies. They also involve the implementation of safeguards and awareness to protect the private data and anonymity of participants when data are shared publicly. Moreover, bespoke visualizations that accommodate the study design, data singularities, and specific models, call for the researcher to understand the grammar of graphics, to know how to modify existing solutions and create unique figures. Beyond creating appealing visualizations, it is also key to seek that the results are accessible and useful to as many people as possible.

Psych 598: Proseminar in Antiracist Science Racism is a system of power, privilege and dominance which advantages White individuals and White communities at the expense of non-White individuals and communities (Feagin & McKinney, 2003; Harrell, 2000). Although psychological science is considered objective, racism exists within psychological research (Buchanan et al., 2021; Roberts et al., 2020; Roberts & Rizzo, 2021). Antiracism includes a critical understanding of racism, Whiteness, and White privilege, and consistent behaviors that challenge racism (Helms, 2017). “Anti-racist research involves understanding and situating racism within societal systems and policies and conducting research that aims to challenge and eradicate racism. Anti-racist research is thus essential to the work of dismantling systems of racism and oppression” (Wray-Lake et al., 2022, p. 1286). Psych 598 is a multi-year proseminar designed to educate faculty and students on conducting antiracist psychological research. Invited speakers will come from subdisciplines within the field of psychology.
